abstract: |
  The Penn State Worry Questionnaire (PSWQ) is a widely used 16-item measure of
  trait worry, and its psychometric literature has reached markedly different
  conclusions about the structure and dimensionality of the instrument. We
  suspect that much of this divergence reflects how studies interpret model fit,
  and in particular a reliance on rule-of-thumb cutoffs, together with variation
  in the choice of estimator for confirmatory factor analysis and in whether and
  how local independence of the items is evaluated. This protocol describes a
  scoping review that maps the psychometric literature on the PSWQ published
  since 2010 and charts not only what each study concluded but how it reached
  that conclusion. Eligible records are empirical studies that report an original
  psychometric evaluation of a PSWQ version that evaluates a specified
  structure, including Rasch measurement theory, item response theory, and confirmatory factor
  analysis. Any population and
  setting are included, and
  eligibility is limited to reports written in English. The search pairs an
  instrument-only search for sensitivity with an instrument-and-methods search
  for precision, run across open databases (OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Europe
  PMC, and PubMed). For each
  study we chart the method, estimator, and dimensional conclusion, together
  with the criteria used to interpret model fit, and we record whether
  and how each of four measurement properties, unidimensionality, local
  independence, invariance, and ordered response-category thresholds, was
  evaluated. Findings will be summarized descriptively rather than pooled.
---

## Background {#sec-background}

The 16-item Penn State Worry Questionnaire (PSWQ) is one of the most widely used
self-report measures of trait worry. It has a large psychometric literature, and
that literature has reached markedly different conclusions about the structure
and dimensionality of the instrument, from a single worry factor to correlated
two-factor and method-factor solutions [e.g @wilsonComparisonLongShort2025].

A shortcoming that affects psychometric studies across all methods is the use of
rule-of-thumb cutoffs to interpret model fit. Fixed thresholds for fit indices
were never meant as universal decision rules, and a growing body of work shows
that they misclassify fit under conditions that are common in questionnaire data
[@marshSearchGoldenRules2004; @mcneishDynamicFitIndex2021;
@goretzkoEvaluatingModelFit2024; @mcneishHowPsychologistsDetermine2026;
@johanssonDetectingItemMisfit2025;@groskurthWhyWeNeed2024]. We suspect that reliance on these cutoffs is
a major reason for the divergence in the PSWQ literature. Two further sources of
variation are the choice of estimator in confirmatory factor analysis and
whether, and how, local independence of the items is evaluated.

Within modern psychometrics, four properties are usually described as
prerequisites for measurement [@christensenPsychometricValidationPROM2021]:

- unidimensionality
- local independence
- invariance across relevant groups
- monotonicity, in the sense of ordered response-category thresholds

These four properties organize the review. Together they are conditions for a
total score to be interpretable as a measure of one latent variable with a
constant meaning across groups. Sufficiency in the stricter sense, where the
total score carries all the information the responses hold about the person
parameter, belongs to the Rasch family and not to the other models in scope
[@kreinerValidityObjectivityReflections2007]. Elsewhere the optimal score weights
items by discrimination in item response models and by standardized factor
loadings in factor models [@mcneishPracticalImplicationsSum2024]. Not every
property is addressed by every method. The ordering of response-category
thresholds can be evaluated only with adjacent-category models, which is to say the partial credit model, the
rating scale model, and the generalized partial credit model
[@andrichExpandedDerivationThreshold2013]. Confirmatory factor analysis does not
address the property at all, and the boundary
parameters are ordered by construction in the graded response model. As a result, disordered thresholds cannot be identified, even if they are present in the data. Charting which properties each
study evaluated, and how, is therefore as informative as charting the conclusions
the studies reached.


## Review objectives and questions

The objective is to map the psychometric literature on the PSWQ published since
2010, to describe how that literature has evaluated the instrument, and to
examine whether interpretive choices are related to the divergent conclusions on
structure and dimensionality. The review addresses four questions.

1. Which psychometric methods and models have been applied to the PSWQ since
   2010, and in which populations, languages, and versions.
2. What conclusions on structure and dimensionality have been reached, and how
   they vary across studies.
3. For each of the four measurement properties in @sec-background
   (unidimensionality, local independence, invariance, monotonicity), whether
   and how the property was evaluated.
4. Which criteria were used to interpret model fit (rule-of-thumb or
   simulation-based), which estimator was used in the factor-analytic models,
   and how local dependence was handled, and whether these choices track the
   structural conclusions reached.

## Eligibility criteria

Framed as Population, Concept, Context (PCC), with further restrictions on
design, timeframe, and language.

- Population. Any sample completing a PSWQ version, with no restriction on age,
  clinical status, or population.
- Concept. A psychometric evaluation that specifies a structure for the PSWQ
  and evaluates its adequacy against criteria, using at least one method in
  scope: Rasch or other item response theory models, confirmatory factor
  analysis, structural equation modeling, exploratory structural equation
  modeling (ESEM), measurement invariance, or differential item functioning.
  ESEM is in scope on this principle, despite its name, since it fits a
  specified number of factors and reports model fit, factor correlations, and
  invariance. Methods that derive the number of dimensions from the data rather
  than evaluating a specified structure are out of scope, including exploratory
  factor analysis, principal component analysis, and exploratory graph analysis
  (EGA). Network models are also out of scope, including confirmatory ones,
  because a network describes relations among the items rather than whether a
  total score measures one latent variable.
- Context. Any setting and country.
- Study designs. Empirical studies reporting an original psychometric evaluation
  of the PSWQ with at least one in-scope method (see Concept). Reviews,
  commentaries, and studies using the PSWQ only as an outcome are excluded.
  Studies that do not evaluate a specified structure for the PSWQ are also
  excluded, whether they report only classical reliability and validity
  correlations or only methods that derive the number of dimensions from the
  data.
- Timeframe. Published 2010 onward.
- Language. Only reports written in English are included. Reports in other
  languages are excluded at the screening stage. This restriction is pragmatic
  and may miss psychometric studies of non-English PSWQ translations that are
  published only in other languages.

## Information sources

The searches use open databases only, chosen after a pilot run of the
instrument-only search. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar carried the field:
together they held almost all of the records that appeared in a single source,
while Europe PMC and PubMed, whose biomedical coverage OpenAlex already spans,
each added only a handful of unique records. OpenAlex is therefore the primary
source, Semantic Scholar the second, and Europe PMC provides biomedical
completeness. PubMed returned seven records that no other source held, and on
inspection none of them was an eligible record the other sources had missed, so
PubMed is retained as a check on biomedical coverage rather than for what it
adds. Scopus and Web of Science are not used, so the search is fully
reproducible by any reader.

The full strategy, per-database strings, and code are in @sec-appendix.

## Search strategy

The instrument block is `"Penn State Worry Questionnaire" OR PSWQ`. A methods
block covering Rasch, item response theory and variants, factor-analytic and
structural equation models, measurement invariance, and differential item
functioning is ANDed with it for the precision search, while an instrument-only
search is run for sensitivity. Database-specific strings, wildcards, and field
tags are documented in full in @sec-appendix so the search is reproducible.
Before the searches are run, each string is checked against a known set of five
to ten PSWQ psychometric papers, and a string that fails to return one of them
is revised and the revision recorded as a new query version in the search log.
The search is reported following PRISMA-S.

## Selection of sources of evidence

Two reviewers screen each title and abstract independently, then full texts, with
disagreements resolved by discussion or a third reviewer. Screening is done in
Rayyan. Inter-reviewer agreement and the reasons for full-text exclusion are
reported in a PRISMA-ScR flow diagram. Two full-text exclusion reasons are
pre-specified, not a PSWQ psychometric study, and no evaluation of a specified
structure for the PSWQ. The second reason covers three groups, studies reporting
only classical reliability or validity correlations, studies reporting only
exploratory methods such as exploratory factor analysis, principal component
analysis, or exploratory graph analysis, and studies reporting only network
models. Records excluded under the second reason are counted at screening and
the three groups are counted apart, since the prevalence of each is itself a
finding. None of them is carried into data charting, which covers studies
evaluating a specified structure.

## Data charting

Two reviewers chart every included study independently, with disagreements
resolved by discussion or a third reviewer. The fields in @tbl-charting record
both the conclusions reached by each study and the methods used to reach them.
The fields for dimensionality, local dependence, invariance, and ordered
response categories correspond to the four measurement properties in
@sec-background, so the review can describe the
evidence behind each conclusion and not only the conclusion itself.

| Field | What is recorded |
|-------|------------------|
| Author | First author |
| Year | Publication year |
| Title | Article title |
| Study population | Sample description, setting, and country. Use a separate row per study when a paper reports more than one |
| N | Sample size |
| PSWQ version | Full 16-item form or a short form (for example PSWQ-A, PSWQ-8, PSWQ-3) |
| Psychometric method(s) / model(s) | CFA, Rasch (PCM, RSM), IRT (GRM, GPCM, or other), ESEM (record the rotation), or a combination |
| Estimator | ML, MLR, WLSMV, or ULSMV for factor models, MML for IRT, and CML, JML, or MML for Rasch |
| Software | For example lavaan, Mplus, Winsteps, eRm, mirt, TAM |
| Dimensionality cutoffs | Rule-of-thumb or simulation-based, and which metrics or indices |
| Dimensionality result | The structural or dimensional conclusion reached |
| Local dependence | Evaluated? Yes or No. Examples: residual/error/Q3 correlations |
| LD cutoffs | Rule-of-thumb or simulation-based, if evaluated |
| LD result | Method used and which item pairs were locally dependent, if any |
| Invariance | Evaluated? Yes or No. Examples: multi-group CFA (MG-CFA), or differential item functioning (DIF) |
| Invariance variable(s) | Which grouping variables were evaluated, such as sex, age group, language version, or clinical status |
| Invariance cutoffs | Rule-of-thumb or simulation-based, if evaluated |
| Invariance result | Groups tested, the finding, and which items showed DIF or non-invariance, if any |
| Ordered response category thresholds | Evaluated? Yes or No. Only evaluable with adjacent-category models (PCM, RSM, GPCM). Not evaluable with CFA, nor with the GRM, where thresholds are ordered by construction |
| Response category result | The finding, such as disordered thresholds |

: Data charting fields. {#tbl-charting}

*Note.* CFA = confirmatory factor analysis; ESEM = exploratory structural
equation modeling; IRT = item response theory; PCM = partial credit model; RSM = rating scale
model; GRM = graded response model; GPCM = generalized partial credit model;
ML = maximum likelihood; MLR = robust maximum likelihood; WLSMV = mean- and
variance-adjusted weighted least squares; ULSMV = mean- and variance-adjusted
unweighted least squares; MML = marginal maximum likelihood; JML = joint maximum
likelihood; CML = conditional maximum likelihood.

## Synthesis

Results are charted and described rather than pooled, so no meta-analysis of
parameter estimates is planned. Reporting is organized around the four
measurement properties in @sec-background and around the three interpretive
choices this review suspects of driving the divergent conclusions, which are the
type of cutoff used to interpret model fit, the estimator chosen for the
factor-analytic models, and whether and how local dependence is evaluated. Those two
outputs are reported first. The descriptive map of methods and populations
supports them and follows.

First, the evaluation of the four measurement properties. The four properties in
@sec-background are conditions for a total score to be interpretable as a
measure of one latent variable, and unidimensionality is one of them, so the
matrix records what each study found and not only what it evaluated. The
study-by-property matrix covers unidimensionality, local independence,
invariance, and ordered response-category thresholds. Each entry records how the
property was assessed, the cutoff or criterion applied where @tbl-charting
records one, and what was found. For local independence, invariance, and ordered
response-category thresholds the prior question is whether the property was
evaluated at all, and counts are reported as the number and percentage of studies
evaluating each one. For unidimensionality the informative entries are how
dimensionality was assessed and what the assessment showed, since findings of
multidimensionality are expected and a departure from unidimensionality bears on
whether a total score measures one latent variable at all. Ordered
response-category thresholds can be evaluated only with adjacent-category models,
so that property is reported against two denominators, all included studies and
the subset fitting a partial credit, rating scale, or generalized partial credit
model. Studies fitting a graded response model count toward the first denominator
and not the second, since its boundary parameters are ordered by construction.

The number of studies that never evaluate local independence is reported on its
own and not only as a row of the matrix. Local dependence inflates reliability
and can produce an apparent second dimension, so a study that does not evaluate
it cannot distinguish a substantive second factor from dependence between items,
and the size of that group bounds how much of the dimensionality literature can
be interpreted at all.

Two of the properties are charted at the item level, and each gets a summary of
its own. For local independence, a table of item pairs counts how many studies
flagged each pair. For invariance, a table of items by grouping variable counts
how many studies found differential item functioning for each combination, which
shows whether particular items carry DIF for a particular variable, such as sex,
across the literature. Item numbers are mapped onto the 16-item version, since
the short forms renumber items, and studies that report a finding without
identifying the items contribute to the property counts but not to the item-level
tables.

Second, the interpretive choices and the structural conclusions. The
dimensionality findings charted in the first matrix are grouped into a small set
of conclusion categories, such as a single worry factor, correlated factors, and
a solution with a method factor for the reverse-worded items, and the
distribution across those categories is reported.
Each category is then cross-tabulated against the type of cutoff used
(rule-of-thumb or simulation-based), the estimator, and the handling of local
dependence. These three tables address the central question of the review,
and they are reported together to allow the reader to see whether studies reaching
different conclusions differ in these methodological choices. They are described, not tested.
Cell counts are expected to be small, and the studies differ in sample size,
population, and PSWQ version, so any pattern is read as descriptive and as a
basis for further work, not as evidence that one choice produced one conclusion.

Third, a map of methods and populations. A matrix of psychometric method by study
population gives the coverage of the literature, supported by counts by PSWQ
version, language of administration, country, and publication year. Each cell
counts study-by-method pairs, so a study applying more than one method
contributes to more than one cell and the row and column totals exceed the number
of included studies. Cells containing no studies are printed as 0 rather than
left blank. The population categories are derived from the charted sample
descriptions rather than pre-specified here, since the descriptions are not known
before charting. A figure of records per year, grouped by method family (factor
analytic, including CFA and ESEM, item response theory, and Rasch), shows
whether the mix of methods has changed since 2010.

Studies reporting more than one sample, or more than one PSWQ version, contribute
one charted row per sample, and every count states whether the unit is the study
or the sample. The narrative closes with the gaps these tables show, in
particular the measurement properties that are rarely evaluated, the interpretive
choices that are rarely justified, and the populations and language versions with
little or no psychometric evidence.

This protocol was registered at OSF before screening begins <https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/BZVGW>. The database searches are planned to be conducted on the 29th of September 2026.
The protocol source, the search notebook, and the record files the notebook
produces are kept in a public GitHub repository, <https://github.com/pgmj/pswq_review>, so that the search can be rerun and the reported counts checked. A GitHub

## Appendix A: Search strategy, databases, and record management {#sec-appendix}

Search A uses the instrument name only, year-filtered, with method screened at
the title and abstract stage, for highest recall. It is run in every database
and its deduplicated output is the set that goes to screening. Search B ANDs the
instrument with a methods block for a smaller, higher-precision set. Search B
does not decide inclusion, since every record found by Search A is screened
whether or not Search B returns it. Its purpose is to size the psychometric
subset in advance, which gives the expected screening load, and to show whether
the methods block reaches the records Search A returns. Search B is run for
OpenAlex, as a filter on the returned titles and abstracts rather than as an API
query, and for Europe PMC. The strings for the other databases are documented so
that the search can be repeated in full. The strings below are shown reflowed
across lines to fit the page. These boolean
queries ignore whitespace between tokens, so the line breaks do not change what
they match. Line breaks are never placed inside a quoted phrase.

The runnable pipeline that executes these searches, with caching, harmonization,
deduplication, and per-source contribution, is the companion notebook
`searches.qmd`, which is the authoritative executable record and is deposited in
the project repository with the record files it produces. The R snippets
below mirror it and run Search A, the instrument-only search. The query blocks
document the full strings, including the methods-restricted Search B that
`searches.qmd` runs in its own Search B section.

### Database selection rationale

For a scoping review of a single, narrowly named instrument, an open-only core
is defensible. OpenAlex now indexes well over 250 million works, ingesting
Crossref and PubMed and much of what Scopus and Web of Science cover, and recent
coverage comparisons find it matches or exceeds those databases for most fields.
Open databases also give a reproducibility advantage: any reader can rerun an
OpenAlex or Europe PMC query, whereas Scopus and Web of Science results are gated
behind subscriptions.

The trade-offs are metadata quality rather than coverage. OpenAlex abstracts
come from an inverted index and are sometimes thin or missing, author keywords
are less consistently captured than Web of Science Keywords Plus or Scopus
indexing, and there is no controlled vocabulary to catch idiosyncratic wording.
Search A is robust to this because it does not depend on the methods terms
appearing in a well-populated abstract. Search B is more exposed, so any record
found by A but not B is retained for screening regardless.

A pilot run of the instrument-only search fixed the source set. OpenAlex
contributed by far the most records found in no other source, Semantic Scholar a
smaller but real share, and Europe PMC and PubMed only a handful each. The
seven records unique to PubMed were inspected one by one. Two were irrelevant on
the title, two carried no title, and three carried no DOI, so none of them was an
eligible record that the other sources had missed. The adopted strategy
is therefore open only: OpenAlex as the primary source, Semantic Scholar as the
second, and Europe PMC for biomedical completeness.

### Building blocks

#### Instrument block

```
"Penn State Worry Questionnaire" OR PSWQ
```

The full name plus the acronym also capture the brief variants (PSWQ-A, PSWQ-C,
PSWQ-3, PSWQ-8, PSWQ-PW), since those papers name the parent instrument.

#### Methods block

```
Rasch OR "item response theory" OR IRT OR "graded response model"
OR "partial credit model" OR "rating scale model"
OR "factor analysis" OR "factor analytic"
OR "confirmatory factor analysis" OR "exploratory factor analysis" OR EFA OR CFA
OR bifactor OR "bi-factor" OR "structural equation model*"
OR "measurement invariance" OR "differential item functioning" OR DIF
OR dimensional* OR unidimensional* OR psychometric*
```

`psychometric*` is ANDed with a very specific instrument, so it adds recall with
little noise. For maximum sensitivity append `OR validation OR validity OR
reliability`, accepting more alpha-only studies to screen out. Terms for
exploratory methods are kept although exploratory-only studies are not charted,
since Search B is a size estimate rather than an inclusion filter. The groups
counted apart at screening are identified from the Search A set, so the block
does not need a term for every excluded method.

### Database strings

#### OpenAlex

OpenAlex has no wildcard truncation (search stems, so plurals mostly resolve),
and nested parentheses are unreliable. Comma-separated `filter=` clauses are
combined with AND, so each concept goes in its own `.search` clause with internal
`OR`. The URLs below are shown wrapped for the page. Join each into a single line
and percent-encode spaces and quotes before use (` ` to `%20`, `"` to `%22`), or
use the `openalexR` call, which encodes and paginates for you.

Search A, instrument only (API):

```
https://api.openalex.org/works?filter=
  from_publication_date:2010-01-01,
  title_and_abstract.search:"Penn State Worry Questionnaire" OR PSWQ
  &per-page=200&mailto=magnus.johansson.3@ki.se
```

Search B, instrument AND methods (API):

```
https://api.openalex.org/works?filter=
  from_publication_date:2010-01-01,
  title_and_abstract.search:"Penn State Worry Questionnaire" OR PSWQ,
  title_and_abstract.search:Rasch OR "item response theory" OR IRT
    OR "graded response model" OR "partial credit model"
    OR "rating scale model" OR "factor analysis"
    OR "confirmatory factor analysis" OR "exploratory factor analysis"
    OR bifactor OR "structural equation modeling"
    OR "measurement invariance" OR "differential item functioning"
    OR psychometric
  &per-page=200&mailto=magnus.johansson.3@ki.se
```

```r
library(openalexR)
options(openalexR.mailto = "magnus.johansson.3@ki.se")   # polite pool

# Search A, instrument only. openalexR v2.0.0 renamed some columns (abstract
# `ab` -> `abstract`), so tidy code downstream accepts both names.
oa_raw <- oa_fetch(
  entity = "works",
  from_publication_date = "2010-01-01",
  title_and_abstract.search = '"Penn State Worry Questionnaire" OR PSWQ',
  verbose = FALSE
)

# Search B is approximated by filtering the returned title and abstract locally
# against the methods terms, since OpenAlex returns abstracts. See searches.qmd.
```

### Additional open databases

Each database has its own syntax for fields, phrases, wildcards, and year limits.
The methods block is adapted per database. Wildcards are kept where supported and
spelled out where they are not.

#### Europe PMC

Free, covers biomedical plus preprints. A non-field-qualified query also matches
full text for open-access articles, which inflates counts, so the instrument and
methods terms are restricted to title and abstract with `(TITLE:x OR ABSTRACT:x)`
clauses. The REST API is queried with `resultType=core` to retrieve abstracts in
bulk.

Query (Search A, instrument only):

```
(TITLE:"Penn State Worry Questionnaire" OR ABSTRACT:"Penn State Worry Questionnaire"
 OR TITLE:PSWQ OR ABSTRACT:PSWQ)
AND (PUB_YEAR:[2010 TO 2026])
```

For the methods-restricted Search B, each methods term is wrapped in the same
`(TITLE:term OR ABSTRACT:term)` form and ANDed with the instrument clause.

```r
library(httr2)

epmc_tiab <- function(terms)
  paste(sprintf('(TITLE:%s OR ABSTRACT:%s)', terms, terms), collapse = " OR ")
instrument_epmc <- epmc_tiab(c('"Penn State Worry Questionnaire"', 'PSWQ'))

# resultType=core returns abstractText; paginate with cursorMark.
epmc_core_search <- function(query, page_size = 1000) {
  base <- "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search"
  out <- list(); cursor <- "*"
  repeat {
    resp <- request(base) |>
      req_url_query(query = query, resultType = "core", format = "json",
                    pageSize = page_size, cursorMark = cursor) |>
      req_retry(max_tries = 3) |> req_perform() |> resp_body_json()
    hits <- resp$resultList$result
    out  <- c(out, hits); nxt <- resp$nextCursorMark
    if (length(hits) == 0 || is.null(nxt) || identical(nxt, cursor)) break
    cursor <- nxt
  }
  out
}

epmc_raw <- epmc_core_search(
  paste0('(', instrument_epmc, ') AND (PUB_YEAR:[2010 TO 2026])')
)
```

#### PubMed

Free. Field tag `[tiab]` restricts to title and abstract, `[pdat]` to publication
date. PubMed truncation with `*` does not combine cleanly inside a quoted phrase,
so the modelling variant is spelled out. The query below is Search B. The
programmatic pull beneath it runs Search A, the instrument-only form.

Query (Search B, instrument AND methods):

```
("Penn State Worry Questionnaire"[tiab] OR PSWQ[tiab])
AND (Rasch[tiab] OR "item response theory"[tiab] OR IRT[tiab]
     OR "graded response model"[tiab] OR "partial credit model"[tiab]
     OR "rating scale model"[tiab] OR "factor analysis"[tiab]
     OR "confirmatory factor analysis"[tiab] OR "exploratory factor analysis"[tiab]
     OR bifactor[tiab] OR "structural equation modeling"[tiab]
     OR "structural equation modelling"[tiab] OR "measurement invariance"[tiab]
     OR "differential item functioning"[tiab] OR psychometric*[tiab])
AND 2010:2026[pdat]
```

```r
library(rentrez)

term <- paste0('("Penn State Worry Questionnaire"[tiab] OR PSWQ[tiab]) ',
               'AND 2010:2026[pdat]')

# Fetch summaries via the web history in POST batches; a long id list in a GET
# overflows the URL (HTTP 414).
srch <- entrez_search(db = "pubmed", term = term, retmax = 0, use_history = TRUE)
recs <- list()
if (srch$count > 0)
  for (start in seq(0, srch$count - 1, by = 200)) {
    recs <- c(recs, entrez_summary(db = "pubmed", web_history = srch$web_history,
                                   retstart = start, retmax = 200,
                                   always_return_list = TRUE))
    Sys.sleep(0.34)   # stay under 3 requests/second without an API key
  }
```

#### Semantic Scholar

Free Graph API. The bulk-search endpoint takes a boolean query where `+` is AND,
`|` is OR, `-` is NOT, `"..."` is a phrase, `*` truncates, and `()` groups.
Matching is exhaustive rather than relevance-ranked, which suits a systematic
search. The query below is Search B. The programmatic pull beneath it runs
Search A, the instrument-only form.

Query (Search B, instrument AND methods):

```
("Penn State Worry Questionnaire" | PSWQ)
+ (Rasch | "item response theory" | IRT | "graded response model"
   | "partial credit model" | "rating scale model" | "factor analysis"
   | "confirmatory factor analysis" | "exploratory factor analysis"
   | bifactor | "structural equation model*" | "measurement invariance"
   | "differential item functioning" | psychometric*)
```

```r
library(httr2)

# Instrument-only Search A, paginated over the bulk endpoint's continuation token.
fetch_page <- function(token = NULL)
  request("https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/search/bulk") |>
    req_url_query(query = '"Penn State Worry Questionnaire" | PSWQ',
                  year = "2010-", fields = "title,year,externalIds",
                  token = token) |>
    req_retry(max_tries = 3) |> req_perform() |> resp_body_json()

s2_raw <- list(); tok <- NULL
repeat {
  pg <- fetch_page(tok); s2_raw <- c(s2_raw, pg$data)
  tok <- pg$token; if (is.null(tok)) break
}
```

### Deduplication and PRISMA counts

Each source returns a different column layout, so records are first harmonized to
a common schema, then deduplicated on DOI with a normalized-title fallback. The
per-source and pooled counts feed the PRISMA flow diagram.

```r
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)

# Each source above is tidied to columns source, doi, title, year, abstract
# (the per-source tidy code is in searches.qmd), then combined:
records <- bind_rows(oa_tidy, epmc_tidy, pm_tidy, s2_tidy) |>
  mutate(
    doi_key   = na_if(str_remove(str_to_lower(doi), "^https?://(dx\\.)?doi\\.org/"), ""),
    # Unicode letter and number classes, so non-Latin titles keep a usable key.
    # An ASCII-only class reduces them to "", and records sharing "" collapse.
    title_key = na_if(str_squish(str_replace_all(str_to_lower(title),
                                                 "[^\\p{L}\\p{N}]+", " ")), ""),
    match_key = coalesce(doi_key, title_key)   # DOI where present, else title
  )

identified_by_source <- count(records, source, name = "n_identified")

# Deduplicate, preferring the copy that carries an abstract.
deduped <- records |>
  mutate(has_abs = !is.na(abstract) & abstract != "") |>
  arrange(match_key, desc(has_abs), source) |>
  distinct(match_key, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(-has_abs)

n_identified  <- nrow(records)
n_after_dedup <- nrow(deduped)
n_duplicates  <- n_identified - n_after_dedup

# Per-source unique contribution, the evidence for the source set.
key_source <- distinct(records, match_key, source)
source_contribution <- key_source |>
  count(source, name = "n_records") |>
  left_join(
    key_source |> add_count(match_key, name = "n_src") |>
      filter(n_src == 1) |> count(source, name = "n_unique"),
    by = "source"
  ) |>
  mutate(n_unique = coalesce(n_unique, 0L))
```

Exact keys miss near-duplicates with different DOIs and minor title variants. For
those, `synthesisr::find_duplicates(records$title_key, method = "string_osa")`
flags fuzzy pairs to review by hand before removal. Keep the reconciliation
manual so nothing is dropped silently.

```r
# PRISMA-ScR flow counts. The screening rows are filled during screening.
prisma <- tibble::tribble(
  ~stage,                               ~n,
  "Records identified (all sources)",   n_identified,
  "Duplicates removed",                 n_duplicates,
  "Records screened (title/abstract)",  n_after_dedup,
  "Records excluded at screening",      NA_integer_,
  "Reports sought for retrieval",       NA_integer_,
  "Reports not retrieved",              NA_integer_,
  "Reports assessed for eligibility",   NA_integer_,
  "Reports excluded (with reasons)",    NA_integer_,
  "Studies included",                   NA_integer_
)

identified_by_source
prisma

# Hand the deduplicated set to screening (Rayyan imports CSV/RIS):
# readr::write_csv(deduped, "records_deduped.csv")
# The PRISMA2020 package renders the flow diagram from `prisma` once complete.
```
